cells.tense: You are here at the table with the pen, looking at what your hands have made.
cells.ask: Say out loud one thing this practice has built in you, and who it's for.
cells.core:
You've kept at this long enough that something has actually grown. The repetition stopped being effort a while back and became part of how you move, and what it produced is right there in front of you. You can look at it and know what it cost, without flinching from it or talking it up.

The fairness in this is plain. You know what you owe the people who helped and what you're owed for the hours, and you don't have to wrestle with it to know. That's the clean version of getting something back. Not everything you've grown is a result you planned, though — some of it arrived while you were doing something else, and it counts just the same. Gather it anyway.
cells.sheetLine: You kept at it, and what it built is finally visible.
cells.verb: gathering what the change grew and seeing what it made
cells.place: a place of steady practice, kept by repetition

cells.tense: You'll be working out how you'll say it before the thing is anywhere near finished.
cells.ask: Leave one finished piece alone for a week without bettering it.
cells.core:
You're pressing out ahead of your own work. Somewhere down the road sits the finished version, and you already live there, so what exists now reads as something you haven't earned the right to show. The line keeps moving, and the point of finishing gets shoved in front of you again.

Practice gets built by repetition, and repetition needs passes that are over. When every round gets held back for one more improvement, there's nothing solid for the next round to stand on. That's what the pressing costs. Patience here only works on something you're willing to call done. It doesn't have to be good. It has to exist, unexamined, long enough for your hands to learn it before your head gets another look at it.

cells.tense: There was a stretch when you put the time in like clockwork, and you are still standing where it left you.
cells.ask: Ten minutes of the practice today, aiming at nothing, before anything else gets done.
cells.core:
The practice has gone quiet. Not abandoned — the habit is still in your hands — but the hours stopped going anywhere, and what you were working toward sits unchecked. Why it thinned out, nothing here can say, and this reading can't either. What shows is the work running small and steady, and something that used to come out of it no longer coming out.

Solitary practice runs down like this. Nothing breaks and nothing fails; attention went elsewhere, and the thing you used to make stopped getting made. Skill isn't the gap, and patience isn't either. What's gone is pull — wanting to do the work itself, which is what puts your hands in motion. Ten minutes of that lights more than a whole day of going through the motions.
cells.sheetLine: The practice is still there. The pull running through it isn't.
cells.verb: gathering what the change grew and seeing what it made

no visible act in the ask — could a camera see it?

cells.tense: You are already building the thing, and you keep calling it just the way you work.
cells.ask: Tell someone the next concrete step you're taking and the date you're taking it.
cells.core:
You've already got a way of going at this that holds up under pressure — the practice holds things in place, and the people around you borrow that steadiness without saying so. You describe it as a habit that happened to you, something to report rather than decide.

Meanwhile the real claim is sitting right there. What you steadily make is yours, and one more round of practice is you choosing to keep it. That choosing goes unsaid, so the person doing it gets no credit from the only one who could give it. Say your next move plainly, as something you're doing on purpose. Then it's down where you can see it, and you can hold yourself to what you wrote.

attempts.check: The least supported claim is in Too Little: that some past room made the offering stop — that is a motive the record does not carry, so I only point at practice that thinned and say I don't know why. A reader could fairly say the routine never stopped and the waiting is just patience; the ask stands either way, because checking the shelves tells them something true about what the work actually made. The sentence serving me more than them is the assembling-line image in Too Much — it sounds good and tells them nothing they'd recognise, so it goes.

attempts.check: The claim the record doesn't carry is in Too Little — that the hours simply dried up from inattention; I name only that the practice thinned and say directly that I can't account for it. A reader could fairly say the routine never thinned, they just stopped judging the yield; the ask still holds, since ten minutes aimed nowhere still tells them whether the pull is there. The line serving me more than them was the shelf-by-the-door image in Too Little, which sounded like insight and showed them nothing of their own week, so it's gone.
